measured_against: fair retail value of the vehicle before the damage, taken from a current nationally recognized compilation of retail values, including automated databases. The DOR rule names the NADA Used Car Guide (Southeastern Edition) as an example.
statute_cite: Ala. Code § 32-8-87 (salvage certificates); Ala. Admin. Code r. 810-5-75-.57
summary: Under Alabama's title law, a vehicle is a 'total loss' (salvage) when an insurer or anyone else pays a settlement for damage that equals or exceeds 75% of its fair retail value before the loss. The owner then has 72 hours to apply for a salvage certificate of title. This is a titling rule: it says when the title must be branded, not when an insurer must total a car.
exceptions: Alabama issues its own salvage title only when the total loss occurs in Alabama; losses elsewhere follow the other state's salvage law (per the DOR rule). The 2025 Act described under recent_changes appears to widen this.
A 2012 introduced bill contained language saying that minor theft or vandalism damage is not a total loss. Whether that wording is in the current code is NOT verified.
No model-year or age exemption was found in the sources reviewed. One may exist elsewhere in the title code; not verified.
owner_retention: The owner can keep the car but must apply for a salvage certificate of title within 72 hours of the total loss. A salvage vehicle cannot be registered or driven on public roads until a rebuilt title is issued. An owner who held the car before the salvage event can apply through MyDMV (electronic only) for a rebuilt inspection under § 32-8-87(k)(3). Non-owners need a master dealer regulatory license. DOR lists the fee as $90 ($75 inspection plus $15 title) and needs the salvage title, bills of sale for replaced parts and proof of prior registration. Inspections are usually scheduled 1-2 weeks after the application.

statute_cite: Ark. Code Ann. § 27-14-2301 et seq. (Disclosure of Damage and Repair on the Certificate of Title); DFA Rule 2007-8 (006.05.07 Ark. Code R. 007)
summary: Under Arkansas's title-disclosure law, a vehicle is 'salvage' when an occurrence (collision, theft, vandalism, storm, flood and similar) causes damage equal to or above 70% of its average retail value. The title must then be branded salvage. The law does not apply to vehicles more than seven model years old before the calendar year of the damage, if they were registered in Arkansas at the time.
exceptions: Age exemption: vehicles more than seven model years old before the year of the occurrence are excluded. Per the DFA rule, subtract 8 from the current year to find the latest excluded model year.
The age exemption does not apply to vehicles not registered in Arkansas when damaged; out-of-state salvage brands carry forward regardless of age.
Flood and storm count as qualifying occurrences.
owner_retention: The owner may keep the car with a salvage-branded title. After repair, the owner files the DFA 'Affidavit of Reconstruction of Salvage Motor Vehicle' with the salvage title, and after inspection receives a title branded 'REBUILT'. Official sources found did not name who inspects in-state rebuilds; DMV.org says out-of-state vehicles can be inspected by a certified local officer, Arkansas State Police or an ASP designee. summary: California has no percentage threshold. exceptions: Per the DMV manual, an unrecovered stolen vehicle is not a total loss salvage vehicle.
The DMV can remove a total loss/salvage status only if the insurer reported it in error, shown by a court order or similar proof.
A seller of a total loss salvage vehicle must disclose that status to the buyer.

summary: Connecticut's insurance law defines a 'constructive total loss' as one where the cost to repair, to salvage, or both equals or exceeds the vehicle's value at the time of loss. exceptions: 'SALVAGE PARTS ONLY' applies when 10 or more major component parts (as defined in § 14-149(a)(2)) are damaged beyond repair.

owner_retention: The car may be left with the owner, but registration is cancelled and plates must be removed. Driving a salvage-branded or insurer-declared total-loss vehicle on CT roads is illegal. statute_cite: Fla. Stat. § 319.30 (definitions; salvage)
summary: Florida's title law treats a vehicle as a total loss (salvage) in two ways: when an insurer pays a total-loss claim, or, for an uninsured vehicle, when repairs would cost 80% or more of replacing it with one of like kind and quality. The 80% figure applies to UNINSURED vehicles. For a late-model vehicle (7 model years or newer) worth at least $7,500, FLHSMV declares it unrebuildable and issues a certificate of destruction when repairs reach 90% of current retail value (per FLHSMV procedure TL-36 and 2014 legislation).
exceptions: Where the insurer and owner agree the vehicle will be repaired, it is not treated as a total loss (per search summary of statute; verify wording).
'Late model vehicle' = manufacturer's model year 7 years or newer (2026 statute definition).
The 90% unrebuildable / certificate-of-destruction rule applies only to late-model vehicles with a current retail cost of at least $7,500 before the damage.
Separately defined 'junk' vehicles (worth under $1,000, at least 10 model years old, fit only for parts or scrap) are a different category.
owner_retention: Under ch. 2024-218 (effective 2024-07-01), when the owner keeps a total-loss vehicle, the owner sends the title to FLHSMV within 72 hours after the owner and insurer agree on retention. If the insurer holds the title, it forwards it within 72 hours of receipt. The salvage title can now be issued directly to the owner (form HSMV 82363). Neither party may dispose of the vehicle before getting a salvage title or certificate of destruction. To return it to the road, apply for a rebuilt inspection at an FLHSMV Bureau of Dealer Services regional office or a Private Rebuilt Vehicle Inspection Program facility; the 2022 manual showed a $40 fee. The department must physically examine repaired or replaced major component parts.

measured_against: Economic test: an owner or insurer decides that parts and labor cost minus salvage value makes repair 'uneconomical'. The statute names no value benchmark (ACV/FMV) and no percentage.
statute_cite: Idaho Code § 49-123 (definitions of 'salvage vehicle', 'total loss' and 'rebuilt salvage'; paragraph letters differ between versions, e.g. (2)(o)/(2)(s)); Idaho Code §§ 49-524, 49-525; IDAPA 39.02.05.303
summary: Idaho has no fixed percentage. A vehicle is 'salvage' if it already has salvage paperwork, or if the owner or insurer decides repair is uneconomical once salvage value is taken into account, or if an insurer has paid a total-loss settlement on it. A 'total loss' happens whenever an insurer or anyone else pays the owner because repair is uneconomical. This is a title law. It does not tell insurers when they must total a car.
exceptions: Age and value exemptions for older salvage vehicles were removed by 2006 legislation (HB 660 / HB 727), so all total losses must now get a salvage certificate. This is per an undated ITD release and the 2006 bill pages. The exact effective year was not confirmed.
A VIN inspection is needed for the salvage certificate only when the existing ownership document is from another state (ITD fact sheet).
owner_retention: Yes. When an insurer pays a total loss and the owner keeps the vehicle, the insurer must notify ITD of the payoff within 30 days. The owner must get a salvage certificate before selling or otherwise disposing of the vehicle. After repair, the vehicle may not be driven on Idaho highways until it meets federal safety and emission standards and gets a title branded 'REBUILT SALVAGE' (form ITD 3311, with a salvage vehicle affidavit). Not surrendering the title, or selling without disclosing the total loss, can bring up to 6 months in jail and/or a $1,000 fine (ITD fact sheet).

summary: In Illinois, once an insurer pays a total-loss claim, the insurer is deemed the owner and the vehicle is salvage, whatever the damage percentage. The statute leaves the total-loss decision to the insurer. A separate 70%-of-fair-market-value test (raised from 50% by Public Act 99-932) applies to vehicles of self-insured companies and certain other owners, not to ordinary insured claims.
exceptions: Owner may keep the vehicle, by agreement with the insurer, only if (i) it has hail damage alone that does not affect operational safety, or (ii) it is 9 or more model years old.
Vehicle age is computed as the calendar year of the insurer's payment minus the model year (92 Ill. Adm. Code 1010.550).
Theft total losses: no salvage certificate is needed unless the vehicle is recovered with damage that would itself have made it a total loss (Public Act 100-104).
owner_retention: Only in the two cases above (hail-only damage that does not affect safety, or 9+ model years old) and only if the insurer agrees. Secondary sources say a retained total loss is still salvage and cannot be driven on Illinois roads, and that the insurer must send the title and salvage application to the Secretary of State within 20 days. Neither point was confirmed in primary text. To return a salvage vehicle to the road, the owner applies for a rebuilt title. The Secretary of State inspects any vehicle 8 model years old or newer before the rebuilt title is issued (625 ILCS 5/3-308, seen in an older text). Bills of sale for essential parts are required.

summary: Indiana requires a salvage title for vehicles from the last seven model years that meet one of three triggers. The triggers are: an insurer decides repair is economically impractical and settles the claim; the vehicle is flood damaged; or, for a self-insured owner or someone who bought the vehicle already damaged, repair costs exceed 70% of fair market value. For ordinary insured claims, the trigger is the insurer's own decision, not the 70% figure.
exceptions: Only vehicles within the last seven model years must get a salvage title. The BMV may issue one for older vehicles at the owner's request.
The 70% repair-cost test applies only to self-insured owners and to people who acquired the vehicle after it was damaged.
Flood-damaged vehicles are a separate trigger, and rebuilt flood vehicles carry 'REBUILT FLOOD DAMAGED VEHICLE'.
owner_retention: A salvage-titled vehicle cannot be registered until it gets a rebuilt title. After repair, the owner applies to the BMV for a title with a rebuilt designation ('REBUILT VEHICLE', or 'REBUILT FLOOD DAMAGED VEHICLE'). The application uses the BMV Affidavit of Restoration, which includes a physical inspection by an Indiana police officer, who may charge a fee. One consumer guide says no inspection is required, which conflicts with the statute and form. Failing to apply for a required salvage title is a Class A infraction. The search did not show the specific procedure when an owner keeps an insurer-totaled car.

summary: Iowa treats a vehicle as 'wrecked or salvage' when the cost of repair exceeds 70% of its fair market value before the damage. This applies only to vehicles worth $500 or more before damage. The threshold was 50% until Senate File 230 (signed April 2, 2021, effective July 1, 2021) raised it to 70%. This is a title-branding rule, not a rule about when an insurer must total a car.
exceptions: Applies only to vehicles with a pre-damage fair market value of $500 or more. Per the search excerpt the $500 sentence is in § 321.52(4); confirm which paragraph.
Transition: per the Iowa DOT memo, a salvage title issued before July 1, 2021 for damage between 50% and 70% cannot be reissued under the new law and stays branded salvage.
No model-year cutoff tied to the 70% test was found. A 12-model-year/$1,000 provision for recyclers appears in a separate paragraph.
owner_retention: A salvage vehicle carries a salvage title. To return it to the road, the owner repairs it and passes a salvage theft examination by a listed law-enforcement agency, which checks for stolen parts and confirms ownership. The DOT Help Center lists the fee as $30, while a rules notice says the statutory fee is $50; confirm. The owner then receives a regular title marked 'REBUILT-IA'. Older 'Prior Salvage' Iowa titles convert to 'Rebuilt' on transfer. An insurer holding title may submit an insurer's certification in place of the theft exam.

summary: Kansas defines a 'late model' vehicle (current model year plus the six preceding years) as salvage when repair costs reach 75% or more of its fair market value just before the damage. Exterior cosmetic hail or windstorm damage is excluded. Any vehicle an insurer totals and takes title to is also salvage. The Kansas Insurance Department reads K.S.A. 8-197 as requiring insurers to declare a total loss when a late-model vehicle hits this salvage test, so the rule works as both a title rule and a claims rule.
exceptions: The 75% test applies only to 'late model' vehicles: current model year plus the six preceding model years.
Damage that is only exterior cosmetic damage from windstorm or hail does not count.
Bulletin 2015-1 says the 75% test should use actual repair costs where known.
owner_retention: A salvage-titled vehicle receives a 'salvage title' from the Kansas Division of Vehicles. Once rebuilt, it can get a 'rebuilt salvage' title. statute_cite: KRS 186A.520 (salvage titles); KRS 186A.555 (hail-damaged vehicles); KRS 186A.530 (rebuilt, water-damaged and junk vehicles); 601 KAR 9:200
summary: Kentucky requires the owner to get a salvage title when the cost of parts and labor to restore the vehicle exceeds 75% of its retail value under a nationally accepted used-car guide. The cost of reinstalling deployed airbags is left out of that test. Kentucky also ties insurer payments to this test: insurers may not pay a claim at or above 75% of value until the title is surrendered or a salvage title applied for. A 2005 enactment put that rule in KRS 186A.555 (current wording not re-checked).
exceptions: Airbag reinstallation costs are left out of the 75% test but still count in the insurer's physical-damage estimate. The insurer's total payment may not exceed retail value.
Hail-damaged vehicles are handled under KRS 186A.555 ('Titles of hail-damaged vehicles'), which KRS 186A.520 names as an exception.
KRS 186A.530 notification provisions do not apply to vehicles more than 10 model years old. It was not confirmed whether that age limit extends to the salvage-title requirement itself.
owner_retention: An owner who keeps the vehicle must get a salvage title, and a vehicle cannot be registered for highway use while a salvage title is in force. No certified inspection is needed for the salvage title itself. After repair, the owner applies for a rebuilt title. A Kentucky certified inspector must inspect the vehicle under KRS 186A.115 and 601 KAR 9:090, and the owner submits the TC 96-215 affidavit with original parts receipts. Kentucky State Police may do a confidential inspection if documents are missing. The Transportation Cabinet prints a brand on the title. Water-damaged vehicles require a salvage title and later carry a water-damage brand. The Rebuilt Section is at (502) 564-1257.

summary: Louisiana's vehicle title law defines a 'total loss' as damage equal to 75% or more of market value under the current NADA handbook. A vehicle declared a total loss in an insurance settlement must get a salvage title. Within 30 days of settling the claim, the insurer, its agent or the owner must send the endorsed title and salvage-title application to the Office of Motor Vehicles.
exceptions: Hail: cosmetic hail damage (dents, body damage) at or above 75% gets a hail-damage brand instead of salvage (per a search summary of legislative text; full conditions not read).

OMV policy says that if a vehicle is rebuilt before a salvage title is obtained, the rebuilt application is held until a salvage title is requested. A rebuilt salvage vehicle receives a 'reconstructed' title. The definition and inspection steps were not read in primary text. Water-damaged total losses may be barred from reconstructed titles; that comes from bill text and enactment was not confirmed.

summary: Maine law sets no damage percentage. A vehicle becomes 'salvage' when an insurer or owner declares it a total loss, or when it goes to a recycler or salvage dealer. After settling a claim on a titled vehicle it handles as salvage, an insurer must surrender the title and apply for a certificate of salvage within 30 days.
